Floating-point numbers can represent only a finite subset of the real numbers, and each arithmetic result is rounded to fit back into the available bits of significand. This rounding is the root cause of nonassociativity. When we compute (a + b) + c, the intermediate sum a + b is rounded to the nearest representable value before c is added, and that second addition is rounded again. If instead we compute a + (b + c), the intermediate rounding happens at a different point, on different magnitudes, and the accumulated rounding error generally differs. Because the rounding error depends on the relative magnitudes and signs of the operands at each step, changing the order in which numbers are summed changes which values get rounded against which, and thus changes the final bit pattern of the result. Real numbers obey associativity, but the rounded arithmetic that hardware actually performs does not.

This matters enormously for large matrix multiplications, because each output element is a sum of many products, and that sum is a reduction whose order is not fixed by the mathematical definition of matrix multiplication. On modern hardware, the actual order of accumulation is influenced by many low-level factors: the number of threads or cores used, how work is tiled and scheduled, whether a GPU or CPU is used, the specific BLAS or vendor library implementation, whether fused multiply-add instructions are used, vector-width and SIMD grouping, and even nondeterministic scheduling of parallel reductions where partial sums from different threads are combined in whatever order they finish. Each of these can produce a different summation order for the same logical reduction, and each different order can yield a different sequence of rounding decisions, hence a different final floating-point value—even though all implementations are "correct" in the sense of computing the same mathematical quantity to within rounding error.

For a single dot product the discrepancies are tiny, on the order of the machine epsilon times the number of terms, but for large matrices this effect compounds. Deep and wide networks of matrix multiplications, as in neural network training or inference, propagate these small differences through many layers, and nonlinearities or normalization steps can amplify them further. Consequently, running the same model or the same GPU kernel twice, on different hardware, with a different number of threads, or with a different library version, can produce numerically different outputs, even when using the same seeds and the same mathematical operations. This makes bit-for-bit reproducibility difficult unless the summation order is explicitly fixed, deterministic algorithms are used, or higher precision accumulation is employed to reduce the sensitivity to reordering.

Floating-point numbers approximate real numbers using a fixed number of significand bits, so every arithmetic operation may require rounding the true mathematical result to the nearest representable value. Addition is especially sensitive to this because the magnitudes of the two operands determine how much precision is lost. When two numbers of very different magnitude are added, the smaller one may be shifted so far right during alignment that some or all of its significant bits fall off the end of the significand and are rounded away. This means that the order in which numbers are summed changes which intermediate values are large and which are small at each step, and therefore changes which bits get rounded off. Mathematically, real-number addition is associative—(a+b)+c always equals a+(b+c)—but floating-point addition only approximates this property, and rounding error accumulated in a different order generally produces a different final bit pattern.

This has direct consequences for reproducibility in large matrix multiplications. A single output element of a matrix product is a sum of many products, and modern hardware rarely computes that sum in a fixed, simple left-to-right order. GPUs and multicore CPUs parallelize the reduction across threads, warps, or vector lanes, splitting the terms into groups that are summed independently and then combined. The number of groups, their sizes, and the order in which partial sums are merged depend on the hardware architecture, the number of threads scheduled, the size of the matrices, memory layout, and even runtime factors like thread scheduling and load balancing. Libraries also choose different algorithms (blocked, tiled, tree-reduced, or using fused multiply-add instructions) depending on problem size and available instructions, and specialized units such as tensor cores may accumulate in different precision or grouping than standard vector units. Because each of these choices changes the sequence of pairwise additions, the rounding errors introduced at each step differ, and the final result can differ in the last few bits—or occasionally more, if catastrophic cancellation or very different magnitudes are involved.

For most numerical purposes these differences are negligible, since they are on the order of machine epsilon per operation. But when results must be bit-for-bit reproducible—for debugging, regulatory compliance, or exact replication of experiments across different GPUs, different thread counts, or different library versions—this non-associativity becomes a real obstacle. Achieving reproducibility then requires deliberately fixing the reduction order, using deterministic algorithms, or using higher-precision or compensated summation methods, all of which typically sacrifice some performance to guarantee that the same sequence of additions is performed every time.

When two floating-point numbers of different magnitudes are added, the smaller number's mantissa must be shifted to align exponents, and bits that fall below the precision limit are rounded or truncated. # Floating-Point Addition and Associativity

Floating-point arithmetic on modern hardware follows the IEEE 754 standard, which represents numbers with finite precision using a fixed number of bits for the mantissa and exponent. This discrete representation means that not all real numbers can be represented exactly, and arithmetic operations must round results to the nearest representable value. This fundamental constraint breaks one of the most basic properties of mathematics: the associativity of addition.

When we add three floating-point numbers, the order in which we perform the operations matters. If we compute (a + b) + c, we might get a different result than a + (b + c). This happens because intermediate results must be rounded to fit into the mantissa's bit width. Consider adding a very large number to a very small number. The small number might be so insignificant compared to the large number that it gets rounded away entirely in the intermediate result. If we add the small numbers together first before combining with the large number, they might accumulate enough to survive the subsequent rounding step. Different orderings of operations therefore produce different final answers, and neither is necessarily "wrong" according to the IEEE 754 standard.

This associativity failure becomes particularly problematic in matrix multiplication, one of the most computationally intensive operations in scientific computing. Matrix multiplication inherently requires summing many products together, and the order in which these partial results are combined significantly affects the final answer. Modern hardware executes these operations in parallel across multiple processors and cores, and the particular reduction order depends on factors like the matrix dimensions, hardware architecture, thread scheduling, compiler optimization decisions, and even system load.

When a matrix multiplication is executed with different reduction orders on different machines, different compilers, or even different runs on the same hardware, the floating-point results diverge. The differences might be small, but they are deterministic given a specific execution path and completely unpredictable without knowing those details. This wreaks havoc on reproducibility. Scientists running the same code on different supercomputers might get slightly different results. Debugging becomes frustrating when results differ between runs. Validating numerical correctness becomes ambiguous when the "correct" answer depends on how many cores you throw at the problem.

Some research communities have addressed this through techniques like compensated summation, which tracks rounding errors, or enforced reduction orders that sacrifice parallelism for determinism. However, the fundamental issue remains: the mathematical abstraction of real number arithmetic that most programmers learn in school is not the same as the concrete reality of floating-point computation. Understanding this gap is essential for anyone working with large-scale numerical computing.

# Floating-Point Addition and Associativity

Floating-point arithmetic on modern hardware does not satisfy the mathematical property of associativity because computers represent numbers with finite precision. When you add three numbers A, B, and C, computing (A + B) + C will generally produce a different result than A + (B + C), even though algebra guarantees these expressions are equivalent. This fundamental characteristic of floating-point computation stems from rounding errors introduced at each operation.

Every floating-point number has a limited number of significant digits. When two numbers of vastly different magnitudes are added, the smaller number's least significant digits may be lost during the operation. For example, adding a very large number and a very small number might cause the small number to vanish entirely because the result rounds back to the original large number. The order in which you combine numbers therefore determines which values get truncated and which get preserved.

When different reduction orders are used in the same floating-point calculation, small rounding errors accumulate differently. Adding numbers from smallest to largest can accumulate rounding error more gradually than adding them in reverse order. These differences are typically tiny in isolation, but they compound when repeated across millions or billions of operations in large matrix multiplications.

The impact on matrix multiplication reproducibility becomes severe when different execution strategies are employed. A matrix multiplication requires summing many products together, and this sum can be computed in multiple ways. A CPU might sum products left to right, while a GPU might sum products using tree reduction where partial sums are combined hierarchically. A vector instruction set might accumulate results in a completely different order than a scalar implementation. None of these approaches is wrong mathematically, but they all produce slightly different floating-point results.

This problem becomes particularly acute in scientific computing and machine learning, where identical computations run on different hardware architectures or even with different compiler optimizations. A training run on one GPU might produce slightly different results than the same training run on a different GPU, even when all other conditions are identical. These differences propagate through subsequent calculations, eventually resulting in completely different outcomes if computations are iterated many times.

For applications requiring deterministic results, such as validating simulations or reproducing research findings, this non-associativity of floating-point arithmetic presents a genuine challenge. Researchers must either accept that floating-point results are inherently system-dependent, constrain computations to a single specific configuration, or use higher precision arithmetic at the cost of performance. Understanding that floating-point addition lacks associativity is essential for comprehending why parallel algorithms produce different answers than sequential ones, and why reproducibility demands explicit attention to computational ordering.

The operation forces alignment of decimal points before addition, and bits that fall outside the allocated mantissa space simply disappear.

Consider what happens when you compute (a + b) + c versus a + (b + c). If b and c are similar in magnitude but much smaller than a, the first grouping might cause c to be lost entirely when added to the already-large sum of a and b. However, adding b and c first creates a slightly larger number that might retain more precision when subsequently added to a. The result: two different final answers, both technically correct within floating-point's precision limits, but numerically distinct.

A matrix multiplication computing the dot product of a row and column involves multiplying corresponding elements and then summing all results. The order in which these products are accumulated dramatically affects the final answer due to the rounding errors accumulating differently depending on reduction order.

Different reduction orders refer to alternative ways of grouping and combining these partial sums. A sequential reduction sums products left-to-right, while a tree reduction might sum pairs, then pairs of pairs, and so forth. Some systems use SIMD operations that add four or eight products simultaneously before combining results. Each approach encounters rounding errors at different points in the computation.

Two systems computing the same matrix product with different reduction orders will produce slightly different results. One computer might sum sequentially while another uses parallel tree reduction, generating non-identical floating-point answers despite performing the mathematically identical operation. This becomes particularly problematic in scientific computing, machine learning, and anywhere numerical results must be verified across different platforms or reproduced for validation purposes.

Floating-point arithmetic on modern hardware fundamentally differs from mathematics in a critical way: addition is not associative. This means that (a + b) + c does not necessarily equal a + (b + c) when computed on a computer. Understanding why this happens and its implications for matrix multiplication is essential for anyone working with numerical computing at scale.

The root cause lies in the finite precision of floating-point representation. Modern computers use the IEEE 754 standard, which represents numbers with a fixed number of bits. When adding two floating-point numbers, the result is rounded to fit within this limited precision. If you add three numbers in different orders, you perform rounding operations at different stages, and these rounding errors accumulate differently depending on the order.

Consider adding a very large number, a medium number, and a very small number. If you add the large and medium numbers first, their sum might be so large that the small number gets rounded away entirely before the final addition. Conversely, if you add the medium and small numbers first, you might preserve more information before combining with the large number. The two final results, while close, will differ in their least significant bits.

This mathematical reality becomes problematic when computing matrix multiplications on modern hardware. A matrix multiplication involves summing many products together. Different computational orders produce different intermediate sums and therefore different rounding sequences. When parallel processors tackle the same matrix multiplication differently—perhaps one thread sums products in order while another uses a tree-reduction pattern for parallelism—they obtain slightly different answers.

This non-reproducibility becomes particularly severe with large matrices. A single matrix multiplication might involve millions of individual floating-point additions. Small rounding errors in one approach can compound differently than in another, leading to noticeable differences in the final result. The problem intensifies when matrix multiplications are chained together, as in deep neural networks or scientific simulations, where output from one operation feeds into the next.

The implications are significant for scientific computing and machine learning. Researchers cannot assume that running the same calculation twice with different CPU scheduling or different numbers of parallel workers will produce identical results. While the differences are often small relative to the magnitude of the results, they can matter greatly in sensitive applications like climate modeling, drug discovery, or financial calculations where consistency and verification are critical.

Modern approaches to managing this include using higher precision arithmetic for accumulation, employing error-correcting techniques, or accepting and documenting the variability as inherent to the platform. Some systems deliberately use reproducible algorithms that enforce a specific reduction order to guarantee consistent results, trading some computational efficiency for determinism and reliability.

This property has significant consequences for large matrix multiplications, particularly on modern hardware such as GPUs, multi-core CPUs, and specialized accelerators, which achieve their speed partly by parallelizing the accumulation of sums. # Floating-Point Addition and Matrix Multiplication Reproducibility

Floating-point arithmetic on modern computers uses the IEEE 754 standard, which represents numbers with finite precision using a fixed number of bits for the mantissa and exponent. This representation introduces rounding errors whenever an operation's result cannot be exactly represented in the available precision. The consequence is that floating-point addition violates the mathematical property of associativity: (a + b) + c does not necessarily equal a + (b + c).

This non-associativity arises because rounding happens after each operation, and the order of operations determines which intermediate results get rounded and when. When we add three numbers in one order, the first addition produces a rounded result that then participates in the second addition. In the alternative order, different numbers are added first, creating different intermediate values that accumulate rounding errors in distinct ways. The magnitudes of these accumulated errors grow larger when adding numbers of very different sizes, since smaller values may be entirely lost when added to much larger ones through a process called catastrophic cancellation.

For matrix multiplication, this property becomes critically important. Computing the product of two matrices fundamentally requires summing many individual products across rows and columns. Different reduction orders—different sequences in which we accumulate these products—will produce subtly different final results due to the rounding errors that accumulate through floating-point addition.

On modern hardware with multiple processors or cores, this becomes a serious reproducibility problem. When executing large matrix multiplications, the order in which partial results are combined depends on how work is distributed across processors and how those processors synchronize their results. Different processor configurations, different numbers of threads, or even different scheduling decisions by the operating system can alter the reduction order. This means the same computation run twice on the same hardware might produce slightly different results, and results will almost certainly differ when run on different machines or with different parallelization strategies.

Ensuring reproducibility requires deliberate effort. One approach involves using reduction strategies that are deterministic regardless of parallelization, sacrificing some performance to guarantee consistent ordering. Another involves using higher precision accumulators than the final output precision, which can reduce error accumulation without changing the order of operations. Some systems employ compensated summation algorithms that track and separately accumulate rounding errors. Without such measures, applications that depend on bit-for-bit identical results—such as scientific simulations used in research papers or regulatory compliance testing—cannot guarantee reproducibility across different computational platforms or when code is reoptimized by compilers.

When we add two floating-point numbers, the exact mathematical sum may not be representable, so the hardware rounds it to the closest value the format allows, typically using round-to-nearest-even semantics in IEEE 754 arithmetic. This rounding step depends on the magnitudes and signs of the specific operands being combined at that moment. If we change the order in which numbers are summed, the intermediate partial sums differ, the rounding errors introduced at each step differ, and the final accumulated result can differ as well. Mathematically, real-number addition is associative, but the rounding function that floating-point hardware applies after each operation breaks that property, since rounding is not a linear operation that commutes with regrouping. A classic illustration involves adding a very large number, a very small number, and another very large number of opposite sign in different orders; depending on the sequence, the small number's contribution may be completely lost to rounding in one order but preserved in another.

This lack of associativity has direct consequences for large matrix multiplications, because each output element of a matrix product is computed as a sum of many products, and that sum is a reduction operation. On modern hardware, such reductions are rarely performed in a fixed, strictly sequential order. Instead, the order depends on factors like the number of parallel threads or cores used, the tiling and blocking strategy chosen by a BLAS library, the vector width of SIMD instructions, the presence of fused multiply-add units, and even runtime scheduling decisions that can vary between executions or between different hardware generations. When the number of threads changes, or when a computation is moved from a CPU to a GPU, or when a library switches its internal algorithm for cache efficiency, the summation order for each dot product changes, and so the rounded intermediate results differ slightly. For matrices of modest size, these differences are usually tiny, often at the level of the last few bits of precision, but they are not strictly zero. When such computations are chained across many layers, as in deep neural network training, or repeated across many iterations, as in iterative solvers, these small discrepancies can accumulate and diverge more substantially over time. As a result, running the same nominal matrix multiplication algorithm on different hardware configurations, thread counts, or library versions can yield results that are numerically close but not bit-for-bit identical, which complicates efforts to achieve exact reproducibility in scientific computing and machine learning workflows.

# Floating-Point Addition and Associativity

Floating-point arithmetic on modern hardware operates under the IEEE 754 standard, which represents numbers using a finite number of bits to encode a sign, exponent, and mantissa. This representation introduces a fundamental limitation: numbers cannot be stored with arbitrary precision. When two floating-point numbers are added, the result is rounded to fit back into this fixed-width format, and this rounding operation is where associativity breaks down.

Consider adding three numbers where their magnitudes differ significantly. If you add a large number to a small number first, the small number's contribution might be entirely lost during rounding because the result must fit into the same number of bits. However, if you add the two small numbers together first, their combined magnitude might be large enough to survive subsequent addition to the larger number. The order in which we combine operands directly affects which information gets discarded during rounding, producing different final results. This is not a flaw in the hardware implementation but rather an inherent consequence of fixed-precision representation and the rounding rules required by the floating-point standard.

Matrix multiplication compounds this problem significantly. A matrix multiplication operation fundamentally involves computing dot products, where each element of the result matrix is the sum of many products. When computing a single result element, the intermediate products must be combined through a sequence of additions. The order in which these products are added determines the intermediate rounding errors accumulated along the way, ultimately affecting the final result.

In large-scale matrix multiplications, different computational strategies naturally produce different reduction orders. A single-threaded computation following row-major order will sum products in one sequence, while a parallel computation distributing work across multiple processor cores might sum products in an entirely different order. One thread might accumulate products in columns while another sums them row-wise. Even more problematically, when using distributed computing across multiple machines, the order of reduction becomes non-deterministic, depending on network latency and scheduling decisions.

This non-associativity creates serious challenges for reproducibility. Running the same matrix multiplication twice on different hardware, with different thread counts, or even on the same hardware with different scheduling, can produce numerically different results. These differences, while typically small individually, can accumulate through multiple layers of computation in deep neural networks or scientific simulations. For scientists and engineers requiring bit-identical reproducibility across runs, this poses a genuine obstacle. Various techniques exist to improve reproducibility, such as using higher-precision accumulators or imposing strict reduction orders, but these typically carry performance penalties. Understanding this fundamental incompatibility between hardware efficiency, floating-point representation, and mathematical associativity remains essential for anyone implementing large-scale numerical computations.

This is a direct consequence of the IEEE 754 standard's requirement that each individual operation be correctly rounded, but correctness at each step does not guarantee that different sequences of steps converge to the same rounded answer.

While such differences are usually small in an absolute sense, they can matter for debugging, scientific verification, and regulatory environments where exact reproducibility is required, motivating techniques like fixed reduction orders, deterministic algorithms, or higher-precision accumulation to mitigate the effects of non-associative summation.

However, if we compute a + (b + c), we first round b + c, then add a. These two paths produce different intermediate rounded values, leading to different final results.

The magnitude differences between numbers being added heavily influence the outcome. When a large number is added to a small number, the small number's least significant bits can get lost entirely during rounding. This phenomenon is called catastrophic cancellation or loss of significance. The order in which we add values therefore matters considerably because it determines which bits get preserved and which get lost.

The result of multiplying a row from one matrix by a column from another requires summing many individual products. Different reduction orders produce different sequences of rounding operations. One approach might sum products from left to right, while another might sum them recursively by pairing intermediate results. A GPU implementation might use a different reduction tree than a CPU implementation, or a distributed system might aggregate results differently than a shared-memory system. Each choice creates a distinct sequence of floating-point operations that, while mathematically equivalent, produces numerically different results due to accumulated rounding errors.

This non-associativity means that the same matrix multiplication computation yields slightly different answers depending on the execution order. These differences, while typically small, can accumulate through subsequent calculations in numerical algorithms, leading to divergent results in scientific simulations or machine learning models. This fundamental constraint breaks mathematical properties we take for granted in pure mathematics, most notably associativity of addition. Understanding why this happens and its consequences for matrix multiplication is crucial for scientific computing.

If we first add the two small numbers together, their sum might be rounded in a way that preserves more information than if we add one small number to the large number first, which could cause the small number to be completely lost due to rounding. The difference between these two orderings can accumulate into significant discrepancies.

Floating-point arithmetic on modern hardware does not obey the mathematical property of associativity, which states that (a + b) + c should equal a + (b + c). This fundamental departure from mathematical ideals stems from the inherent limitations of representing real numbers in finite precision formats like IEEE 754 double-precision or single-precision floating-point numbers.

When floating-point numbers are added, the result must be rounded to fit within the available precision. The rounding error depends on the magnitudes of the numbers involved. When adding three numbers in different orders, the intermediate results differ, leading to different rounding errors accumulating along the way. For instance, if you add a very small number to a very large number first, the small number may be entirely lost to rounding. However, if you add the small number to another small number first, their sum might be large enough to meaningfully contribute to the final result. This order-dependence means that mathematically equivalent expressions produce different numerical results on actual hardware.

This non-associativity creates significant challenges for scientific computing at scale. Matrix multiplication requires accumulating dot products, which are essentially long sequences of additions. When a large matrix multiplication is performed on multiple processors or with different parallelization strategies, the reduction order changes, meaning different processors accumulate partial sums in different sequences. Even when using identical data and algorithms, the order in which intermediate results are combined during parallel reduction trees differs from machine to machine or from run to run.

The practical consequence is that reproducibility becomes impossible to guarantee without explicit constraints. Two supposedly identical runs of a large matrix multiplication executed with different parallelization strategies or on different hardware configurations will produce slightly different answers. The differences may seem tiny, confined to the last few representable bits, but they are real and unavoidable given the current floating-point standard.

For scientific applications demanding reproducible results, researchers have developed workarounds. Some approaches use higher-precision arithmetic for accumulation before rounding final results. Others implement specialized reduction algorithms that enforce a fixed order of operations across all parallel implementations. Some codebases deliberately serialize certain computations or mandate specific reduction orders to achieve bit-for-bit reproducibility, though this often comes at significant performance cost by limiting parallelization opportunities.

Understanding this fundamental limitation helps explain why large-scale scientific simulations sometimes produce slightly different results when scaled to different numbers of processors, and why reproducibility in floating-point computing requires careful, deliberate design choices rather than naive assumptions about the properties of arithmetic.

Floating-point addition fails to be associative because computers represent real numbers with a finite number of bits, using formats like IEEE 754 that encode a sign, exponent, and a limited-precision mantissa. When two floating-point numbers of very different magnitudes are added, the smaller number's mantissa must be shifted to align exponents, and bits that fall below the precision limit are rounded off or discarded. This rounding is not just a minor inconvenience—it means that the result of (a + b) + c can differ from a + (b + c), because the order in which numbers are combined determines which intermediate values get rounded and how much information is lost at each step. Unlike addition over the real numbers, floating-point addition is only associative in special cases, such as when no rounding occurs or when the numbers involved share convenient magnitudes. In general, changing the grouping of operations changes the sequence of rounding errors, producing a different final result.

This property has direct consequences for large matrix multiplications, particularly on modern hardware such as GPUs, TPUs, or multi-core CPUs, where operations are parallelized and reduction orders are often nondeterministic or hardware-dependent. Matrix multiplication involves summing many products to compute each output element, and this summation is a reduction operation. When the reduction is performed sequentially, in tree-like fashion, in blocks, or via parallel threads that finish in unpredictable order, the sequence in which partial sums are combined varies. Because floating-point addition is not associative, these different reduction orders can yield slightly different final results, even though mathematically the sums are identical.

For large matrices, this issue is compounded: many additions occur, so rounding errors can accumulate differently depending on execution order, and running the same multiplication twice on different hardware, different thread counts, or even the same hardware with different scheduling can yield numerically distinct outputs. This makes exact bitwise reproducibility difficult to guarantee across platforms, library versions, or parallelization strategies, which is problematic for tasks demanding strict determinism, such as debugging, certification, or scientific reproducibility. While the differences are usually tiny in absolute terms and often negligible for many applications, they can matter in iterative algorithms where small discrepancies amplify over many iterations, such as training deep neural networks or performing long simulations. As a result, ensuring reproducible floating-point computation typically requires enforcing a fixed reduction order, using deterministic algorithms, or accepting some tolerance in output rather than relying on exact equality across runs.

Although each individual rounding error is tiny, these errors do not cancel out predictably; they accumulate in ways that depend on the exact sequence of operations.

This lack of associativity has direct consequences for large matrix multiplications, which fundamentally involve computing sums of many products (dot products) to produce each output element. In principle, the mathematical result of a dot product does not depend on the order in which terms are summed, but on real hardware it does, because each partial sum is rounded. Modern hardware exacerbates this issue because matrix multiplication is heavily parallelized: different implementations, libraries, or even different runs on the same hardware may split the summation across threads, cores, or vector lanes in different ways, and use tree-reduction, pairwise summation, or sequential accumulation strategies. GPUs in particular often use highly parallel reduction trees whose exact shape can vary with problem size, tiling strategy, or scheduling decisions, and may also employ fused multiply-add instructions that change how intermediate rounding occurs compared to separate multiply and add operations. As a result, the same logical matrix multiplication computation, run on different hardware, different library versions, different thread counts, or even different times on the same hardware if the scheduler behaves nondeterministically, can produce answers that differ in the last few bits of precision.

For most practical purposes these differences are negligible, since they are on the order of machine epsilon and do not affect the overall correctness of computations. However, this lack of bitwise reproducibility becomes significant in contexts where exact numerical determinism is required, such as debugging, verifying scientific results, certifying safety-critical software, or training machine learning models where tiny discrepancies can compound over many iterations, causing divergent training trajectories across supposedly identical runs.
